summary: An informational memo from Ipsilon Networks specifying version 2.0 of the General Switch Management Protocol, which lets a controller manage an ATM switch. It extends the earlier version of GSMP and was written as a vendor description, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2297 describes GSMP, the protocol a controller uses to run an ATM switch. The controller asks the switch to set up connections, manage ports and report statistics, and the switch can also push news about events such as a link going down.

subtitle: How a controller tells an ATM switch to set up connections, report status and offer quality of service.

tldr.problem: An ATM switch needs an outside controller to establish and release connections, manage its ports, and report configuration and statistics.
tldr.mechanism: GSMP is a master-slave protocol: the controller sends request messages and the switch replies with a result and a transaction identifier. An adjacency protocol first synchronizes state and agrees on a version. Version 2 adds the Quality of Service messages.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo from the protocol's authors that updates RFC 1987, and it says it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

today: RFC 2297 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1987, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it further. It describes the protocol for the Internet community and says it specifies no Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: What GSMP Controls
sections.content:
The General Switch Management Protocol is a general purpose protocol to control an ATM switch. It lets a controller establish and release connections across the switch, add and delete leaves on a multicast connection, manage switch ports, request configuration information and request statistics. It also lets the switch inform the controller of asynchronous events such as a link going down. GSMP runs across an ATM link connecting the controller to the switch, on a control connection, a virtual channel, established at initialization. Operation across an Ethernet link is also specified. The protocol is asymmetric, the controller being the master and the switch the slave, and several switches may be controlled by one controller using separate control connections.

A switch is assumed to contain multiple ports, and each port is a combination of one input port and one output port. Some requests refer to the port as a whole, others to the input port or the output port alone. ATM cells arrive at the switch on incoming virtual paths or virtual channels at an input port, and depart on outgoing virtual paths or virtual channels from an output port. Virtual paths on a port or link are referenced by their virtual path identifier, VPI, and virtual channels by their virtual path and virtual channel identifiers, VPI and VCI.

A virtual channel connection across the switch is formed by connecting an incoming virtual channel to one or more outgoing virtual channels, and it is referenced by the input port on which it arrives and the identifiers of its incoming virtual channel. A virtual path connection is formed by connecting an incoming virtual path to one or more outgoing virtual paths, and in such a connection the value of the VCI in each cell is not used by the switch and remains unchanged by it. GSMP supports point-to-point and point-to-multipoint connections. A multipoint-to-point connection is set up as several point-to-point connections that each name the same output branch, and a multipoint-to-multipoint connection as several point-to-multipoint trees that each name the same output branches.

In general a virtual channel is established with a certain quality of service, and version 2 of the protocol introduces a rich set of QoS messages. Operating GSMP with none of the QoS messages is permitted, in which case each connection may be assigned a priority when it is established, and a cell on a higher-priority connection sharing an output port is much more likely to exit the switch first. The number of priorities a port supports can be obtained from the port configuration message. GSMP also contains an adjacency protocol, used to synchronize state across the link, to negotiate which version of GSMP to use, to discover the identity of the entity at the other end of a link, and to detect when it changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol lets one computer act as the manager of an ATM switch. It runs over a dedicated connection between the two, and the manager is always in charge: it asks, the switch answers.

sections.title: Encapsulation and the Message Header
sections.content:
GSMP packets are variable length. On an ATM data link layer they are encapsulated directly in an AAL-5 CPCS-PDU with an LLC/SNAP header, whose octets are 0xAA 0xAA 0x03 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x88 0x0C, where 0x880C is the assigned Ethertype for GSMP. The maximum transmission unit of the GSMP Message field is 1492 octets. The virtual channel over which a GSMP session is established between a controller and its switch is called the GSMP control channel, and the default VPI and VCI for LLC/SNAP encapsulated GSMP messages on an ATM data link layer are VPI = 0 and VCI = 15.

On an Ethernet data link the encapsulation carries the destination and source MAC addresses, the Ethertype 0x88-0C, the GSMP message, a Sender Instance and a Receiver Instance, padding and a frame check sequence. The Sender and Receiver Instance numbers come from the adjacency protocol and are appended to all non-adjacency messages to offer additional protection against the introduction of corrupt state. Padding to the minimum Ethernet frame size of 46 octets of data is added if necessary, and is not part of the GSMP message. After the adjacency protocol has synchronized, a receiver checks the source address, the Sender Instance and the Receiver Instance of every Ethernet-encapsulated GSMP message, and discards the message if the Sender Instance and the source address do not match the values stored by the Update Peer Verifier operation, if it arrives over any port other than the one where synchronization was achieved, or if the Receiver Instance does not match the current value.

All GSMP messages except the adjacency protocol message share one header. The Version field carries the GSMP version negotiated by the adjacency protocol. The Message Type field selects the message; GSMP messages fall into six classes, Connection Management, Port Management, State and Statistics, Configuration, Quality of Service and Events, each with a number of message types, and one type is allocated to the adjacency protocol. The Result field says whether a response is required and, in a response, whether the outcome was success or failure. In a request, NoSuccessAck means no response is expected if the request succeeds, and AckAll means a response is expected; in both cases a failure response must be generated if the request fails. For State and Statistics and Configuration requests, NoSuccessAck is ignored and the request is handled as if it were AckAll, which the memo says was added to reduce control traffic when the controller periodically checks that the switch state is correct. In a response the field has three values: Success, More and Failure, where More means the success response exceeds the maximum transmission unit and that further messages will complete it, and all messages of one success response share the same transaction identifier. The encoding is NoSuccessAck 1, AckAll 2, Success 3, Failure 4 and More 5.

The Code field gives further information about the result, mostly an error code in a failure response. The Transaction Identifier associates a request with its response; the controller may choose any value for a request, a response copies the identifier of the request it answers, and an event message should set it to zero. Fields that are unused or reserved must be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver. Extra data after the end of the message body is not an error, which supports development and experimental purposes, as long as the maximum transmission unit is not exceeded, and a success response must not be sent until the requested operation has actually completed.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts the same way: which version of the protocol, which kind of message, whether it succeeded, and a number that lets the answer be matched to the question. The rest of the message depends on the type.

sections.title: Message Classes, Events and Failures
sections.content:
GSMP is a master-slave protocol. The controller issues request messages and the switch replies with a response message indicating either a successful result or a failure. Each request says whether a response is required and carries a transaction identifier so that the response can be associated with it. There are five classes of request-response message: Connection Management, Port Management, State and Statistics, Configuration and Quality of Service. The switch may also generate asynchronous Event messages, which are not acknowledged by the controller, and there is an adjacency protocol message used to establish synchronization and maintain a handshake.

Each message type has a format for the request and a format for the success response. Unless otherwise specified, a failure response is identical to the request that caused the failure, with the Code field giving the reason. If the switch issues a failure response, no change should be made to the state of the switch as a result of the message that failed, though for requests that contain several requests, such as Delete Branches, the failure response says which succeeded and which failed. When several failures match, the most specific one is chosen, in this order: Invalid Message, a failure specific to the message type, a failure response specified in the text of that message type, Connection Failures, Virtual Path Connection Failures, Multicast Failures, QoS Failures, and General Failures.

Switch ports are described by a 32-bit port number assigned by the switch, whose internal structure is opaque to the protocol but is stable for a port in the same physical place even across power cycles. Each port also maintains a port session number assigned by the switch, which changes when the port returns to the Available state, when the line status comes back up, or after a power cycle. A message with an incorrect port session number must be rejected, with the Code field saying invalid port session number, which lets the controller detect a link failure and keep its state synchronized.

Event messages let the switch report asynchronous events such as a port going up or down, an invalid VPI or VCI, a new port and a dead port. They are not acknowledged, the Result and Code fields are not used and are set to zero, and they are not sent during initialization. Each port keeps an Event Sequence Number, which starts at zero when the port is initialized and is incremented each time the port detects an event, even if flow control prevents the event message from being sent.

Section 12 lists the whole message set and marks the messages that must be supported in a minimal implementation. The required ones are the Adjacency Protocol, Add Branch VCC, Delete Branches, Port Management, Port Statistics, Switch Configuration, Port Configuration and All Ports Configuration. The rest, including Delete Tree, Delete All, Move Branch, the Label Range message, the Connection Activity and Report Connection State messages, the event messages and the whole Quality of Service set, are optional for a minimal implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller asks, the switch answers, and each answer carries a number that matches it to the question. When the switch cannot do what was asked, it sends the request back with a failure code and changes nothing. The switch can also send news about things that happen on its own, such as a port failing.

sections.title: Quality of Service
sections.content:
The Quality of Service messages are the main addition in version 2. They let a controller group virtual path connections and virtual channel connections into QoS classes, and allocate QoS resources both to classes and to individual connections. At initialization the switch describes its QoS capabilities to the controller in terms of the abstract switch model, using the QoS Configuration message. The controller then issues Scheduler Establishment messages to configure the scheduler on each switch output port, and QoS Class Establishment messages to configure the QoS classes. Connections may be added to or deleted from a QoS class using the QoS Connection Management message, and QoS resources may also be assigned to individual connections with that same message. Connections that only need the scheduler can use the simple connection management messages instead.

The abstract switch model is the means by which a switch describes its fundamental QoS capabilities, and it consists of four main functions: a policer, a classifier, a regulator and a scheduler. The classifier groups multiple connections together into a QoS class so that QoS resources may be shared by the class as a whole. Within a QoS class there is no differentiation between members in the QoS resources they receive, but the ordering of cells within each constituent connection must be preserved on exit from the switch. Connections are not required to be aggregated into a class with others, because they may be allocated individual QoS resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Version 2 adds the ability to promise a level of service. The controller can put connections into a class that shares a share of the switch's capacity, and the switch describes what it can do with four named parts: a policer, a classifier, a regulator and a scheduler.

sections.title: The Adjacency Protocol
sections.content:
The adjacency protocol is used to synchronize state across the link, to agree on which version of the protocol to use, to discover the identity of the entity at the other end of a link, and to detect when it changes. GSMP is a hard state protocol, so it matters to detect loss of contact between switch and controller and any change of identity. No GSMP messages other than adjacency protocol messages may be sent across the link until synchronization has been achieved, and messages received on a link that does not have state synchronization must be discarded.

The adjacency protocol message has its own header: Version, Message Type, Timer, an M-Flag, Code, and then Sender Name, Receiver Name, Sender Port, Receiver Port, Sender Instance and Receiver Instance. The version number for the protocol defined in this specification is Version = 2, and the adjacency protocol uses Message Type = 10.

Version negotiation uses the Version field. In a SYN message it always contains the highest version understood by the sender. A receiver that gets a SYN with a version higher than it understands ignores the message, and a receiver that gets a SYN with a version it understands but lower than its own highest replies with a SYNACK carrying the version from the received SYN, which fixes the version used while the adjacency protocol stays synchronized. All other messages use the agreed version.

The Timer field tells the receiver the timer value used by the sender, the nominal time between periodic adjacency protocol messages, given in units of 100ms, and constant for the duration of a session. The M-Flag says whether the sender is a master or a slave, and it stops a master synchronizing with another master or a slave with another slave. The Code field gives the function of the message, with four codes defined: SYN 1, SYNACK 2, ACK 3 and RSTACK 4.

The Sender Name is a 48-bit quantity unique within the operational context of the device, and with the Ethernet encapsulation it must be the source address from the MAC header. The Sender Port is the local port number of the link the message is sent on, and the Receiver Port is what the sender believes that number to be at the far end. The Sender Instance is the sender's instance number for the link, used to detect when the link comes back up or when the identity of the other end changes: it is a 32-bit number guaranteed to be unique within the recent past and to change when the link or node comes back up after going down, and zero is not a valid instance number. The Receiver Instance is what the sender believes the current instance number at the far end to be.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anything else can be sent, the two ends say hello, agree on which version of the protocol to use, and exchange a number that changes every time the link comes back. That way each side knows it is talking to the same equipment it was before.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it assumes physical security on the control link connecting the controller to the switch, and that security issues are not discussed in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo assumes the link between the controller and the switch is physically protected, and says nothing about security beyond that.

fields.desc: GSMP version negotiated by the adjacency protocol.

fields.desc: Failure code in a failure response; unused in a request.

fields.desc: Links a response to the request it answers.

items.label: Adjacency Protocol
items.desc: Required. The handshake that synchronizes the link.

items.label: Add Branch VCC
items.desc: Required. Adds a branch to a virtual channel connection.

items.label: Delete Branches
items.desc: Required. Removes branches of a connection.

items.label: Delete Tree
items.desc: Removes a whole tree of connections.

items.label: Delete All
items.desc: Removes every connection at the switch.

items.label: Move Branch VCC
items.desc: Moves a branch to another output port.

items.label: Port Management
items.desc: Required. Manages the state of a switch port.

items.label: Port Statistics
items.desc: Required. Reads the counters of a port.

items.label: Switch Configuration
items.desc: Required. Reads the configuration of the switch.

items.label: Port Configuration
items.desc: Required. Reads the configuration of a port.

items.label: All Ports Configuration
items.desc: Required. Reads the configuration of every port.

items.label: Scheduler Establishment
items.desc: Configures the scheduler on an output port.

items.label: QoS Class Establishment
items.desc: Creates and configures a QoS class.

items.label: QoS Connection Management VCC
items.desc: Adds or removes a connection in a QoS class.
